claims.text: An MLIP trained on a limited set of explicit ab initio free-energy calculations can substitute for full ab initio molecular dynamics in evaluating fusion and high-temperature thermodynamic properties.
The proposed MLIP workflow will substantially reduce computational cost while retaining sufficient fidelity.
The training calculations will cover both solid and liquid phases.
Corrections or embeddings will be used to account for anharmonic and electron–vibration coupling contributions.
The method is intended to apply over temperatures bracketing the melting point.
Initial elemental and binary tests will define the composition boundaries before extension to multicomponent high-entropy systems.
The MLIP can serve as a surrogate energy landscape that captures structural and vibrational properties needed for accurate free-energy determination.
Training on ab initio data containing vibrational entropy, anharmonicity, and electron–vibration coupling will allow the MLIP to interpolate free-energy surfaces accurately.
MLIP-driven accelerated molecular dynamics or enhanced sampling will reduce computational cost by approximately an order of magnitude relative to full ab initio molecular dynamics.
The MLIP workflow will be significantly less costly than TOR-TILD.
The MLIP workflow will preserve phase free-energy fidelity within acceptable error bounds.
MLIP-derived free-energy differences and thermodynamic observables will be within approximately 10–20% of full ab initio molecular-dynamics values.
The MLIP workflow may require 10% or less of the computational cost of full ab initio molecular dynamics.
The predicted speed and fidelity will extend from elemental and binary systems to multicomponent high-entropy alloys.
Chemical complexity in multicomponent high-entropy alloys may challenge the MLIP's interpolation accuracy.
The method may extend from the melting regime to moderately superheated or supercooled states.
Electron–vibration coupling may be difficult to capture accurately, especially in multicomponent systems with complex electronic environments.
MLIP interpolation accuracy outside the training regime is uncertain.
